results.summary_before: This design implements the control block for an 8-bit CPU based on the SAP-1 architecture. It uses a 6-stage sequential counter and a lookup table to generate control signals from a 4-bit opcode, with outputs for various register and memory control lines as well as a halt signal. Testing involves applying opcodes and monitoring the control signal outputs, optionally using a logic analyzer or slowing the clock. The project is part of a course (ECE 298A) and is intended to be integrated with other CPU sub-blocks.

results.summary_before: This project implements an 8-bit Kogge-Stone adder in Verilog. It takes two 8-bit inputs and produces their sum, but lacks a carry-out so sums above 255 are not representable. The design is intended as a class exercise and includes a testbench that iterates through all input combinations, skipping cases where overflow would occur. No external hardware is required beyond the chip itself.

results.summary_before: This design drives a two-digit 7-segment display to show the hexadecimal representation of an 8-bit input byte. The byte is latched on a rising clock edge when the write enable signal is high, and the display is continuously driven with segment outputs and a digit select signal. Testing requires connecting a 7-segment display and manipulating the input and write enable pins to verify latching and display updates. The project is notable for its simple interface and use of a standard 7-segment display.

results.summary_before: This project simulates an elevator control system that displays floor numbers on a 7-segment display based on switch inputs. The user selects a floor using the board switches, and the display increments or decrements according to the elevator's state (moving up, moving down, or idle). Testing involves using the switches to select floors and observing the display, which requires an external LED display. The design is a simple state machine demonstration with no additional hardware beyond the display.

results.summary_before: This design is a basic PWM controller that generates a pulse-width modulated output on uo[7] when enabled by ui[7]. The six-bit input ui[5:0] sets the duty cycle in manual mode, or the frequency of an internally generated triangular reference when ui[6] is high, producing a breathing effect. It is tested by enabling the output and observing the PWM signal on uo[7] while flipping the input switches. No external hardware is required, though an LED and resistor are suggested for visual feedback.

results.summary_before: This is a 3-stage Dickson charge pump that boosts the input voltage to approximately 9.6 V, with the output divided by two and available on the analog pin ua[0]. It requires a 2 MHz clock signal to operate. In the TT09 shuttle, the analog pin voltage is limited to VDDIO/VDDA, so the output is divided by three instead. The design is tested by applying a clock and measuring the divided output voltage.
